translations.text: I marveled with you, O lovers of Christ, because the new grace of the Gospel was proclaimed through the Old Testament.
My mind was enlightened with yours, because I saw the apostolic writings illuminated by the words of the prophets. I acknowledge the grace so that I may receive the reward.

I saw the new mysteries proclaimed through the old when Abraham made his servant swear an oath at his loins. He had him place his hand beneath his loins and called the God of heaven and earth as witness to his words.
“Place,” he says, “your hand beneath my loins, and I will make you swear by the Lord God, the creator of heaven and earth.”
There is a great question in these words, for this was done on account of the offspring who was to come forth from Jacob’s loins, according to the saying, “A ruler shall not depart from Judah,
nor a leader from his loins.” How can the oath be found to have been sworn by the [?]? For Isaac had been born long before, and the offspring had already come forth.
And when he administered the oath, there was no hope of any other offspring from the blessed man’s loins.
It is clear that Abraham bore within himself the life-giving seed, of whom Paul said, “The promises were given to Abraham and to his offspring.”

And he sets out and explains the matter in the letter to the Galatians: “It was not said,” he says, “‘To you and to your offspring,’ as referring to many, but ‘To you and to your offspring,’ who is Christ.”
It was thus shown that Christ is Abraham’s offspring according to the flesh, and he rightly administered the oath by that offspring.
The question concerning this is how he administered the oath at his loins, since the life-giving flower had already blossomed from him.
For the member had once become an instrument of holiness, and the divine offspring had once dwelt there. For this reason he administered the oath by the temple.
“And whoever swears,” he says, “by the temple swears by the one who has dwelt in it.” As the Life-giver also said concerning the Pharisees:
“Woe to you, blind Pharisees, because you say that whoever swears by the temple is not bound by anything, but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound.
Fools and blind men! Which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? For this reason I tell you: whoever has sworn by the temple swears by the one who has dwelt in it.”
Just as a royal house that has been the king’s dwelling once and [?], even if the king moves away from it, is called royal because it was once dedicated as a royal residence,
so also the patriarch’s member, which had once become an instrument of the coming dispensation, was a temple of the promised goodness.
And the oath was not in vain, but was a true testimony. Thus he administers the oath by the offspring and explains who the offspring is.
“Place,” he says, “your hand beneath my loins, and I will administer to you an oath by the Lord God, the creator of heaven and earth.”
If this is so, Christ our Savior is the Lord and God of heaven and earth.
For the same reason, when various revelations appeared to the holy prophet Zechariah, there was a particular revelation of this kind.
“I lifted up,” he says, “my eyes and looked, and behold, a lampstand of cast gold, and seven lamps upon the lampstand,
and seven openings for the lamps, and seven burning globes, and two olive branches on the right and on the left.”
And I said to the angel who was speaking to me, “Lord, what is this?” For what appeared to the eyes was of one kind, while the interpretation to come was of another kind.
The things that appeared did not signify themselves, but foretold certain other things. The prophet asks, “Lord,” he says, “what might this be?”
If he was asking about what was plainly visible, then he was not asking properly, if he did not even know what the lampstand was and what the olive trees were.
But the prophet seeks to understand not the visible things themselves, but their interpretation. For he says, “What is this?” And the angel says to him:
“Do you not know what this is?” And he says, “No, lord.” With a humble mind he admits his ignorance and learns from the truth.
He too was a brother of the eunuch who heard Philip ask, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
And with a humble mind he says, “How can I understand unless someone guides me?” Likewise, here he says, “Do you not know what this is?” And he says, “No, lord.”
“What are the two olive branches that are on the right and left of the lampstand?” And he explained the olive branches and, along with them, what the lampstand was.
Pay close attention. The lampstand stood in the middle, and the branches were on either side of the lampstand.
But the angel explains that the branches stood not beside the lampstand, but before God, as though the lampstand were a representation of God—or rather, of our Savior and his work in the flesh.
“Do you not know,” he says, “what this is?” And he says, “No, lord.” “These two branches are the two sons of abundance who stand before the Lord God of all the earth.”
We must also pay close attention to this: he says that the lampstand has seven lamps, because of the Lord’s work in the flesh.
Indeed, the lampstand itself was the Lord’s body, and it received the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit as an example for us, not because of any need of its own.
As Isaiah also says, “A shoot will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will blossom from it, and the Spirit of God will rest upon him.”
Which Spirit? Manifold in the effects of its activity, yet an undivided gift in its nature. “And the Spirit of God will rest upon him.”
In the first words he speaks of the essence of the Holy Spirit, for he calls him the Spirit of God. In the words that follow, he calls the effects that he produces in others “spirit.”
“The spirit,” he says, “of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and reverence for God.”
He speaks of the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit that rested upon the Lord’s body.
The six-branched lampstand also depicts this. A lampstand is shown to make clear the illumination brought about by the workings of the Holy Spirit.
To make this still more certain, a little further down he says, “These are the (seven) eyes of the Lord that look upon all the earth.”
Do you see that the seven gifts rested upon the Lord’s body as an example, for the illumination of all the earth?
And to make this still clearer, the evangelist testifies: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”
Where the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High were present from the very beginning of the divine conception, what need was there afterward for the seven workings of the Spirit,
as the disciples of the heretics slanderously claim, saying that only after his baptism did he become worthy to receive the workings of the Holy Spirit?
We do not deny that the Spirit came at that time, but, as the evangelist himself says, “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descend and rest—he is the one.”
“And I have seen,” he says, “and testify that this is the Son of God.” Do you see that he came as a testimony, and not to supply any deficiency?
Pay attention to how the truth interprets itself through itself and has no need of human reasoning. “These,” he says, “are the ones who stand before the Lord of all the earth.”
Zechariah calls the Life-giver the Lord of all the earth, according to the dispensation of his incarnation. Peter, the head of all the apostles, was speaking with Cornelius.
“We,” he says, “know the message that spread throughout Judea.” Before this he had spoken of “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit.”
There he says, “The message that God sent to proclaim peace to the children of Israel.”
He is Lord of all: of those in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld. He is Lord of the visible and the invisible.
John also speaks in agreement with him: “He who came from above is above all.”
But I consider it necessary also to resolve the other objection of the heretics, who listen to the apostle’s words with impious minds,
as though he received his position above all as some reward for the cross, as though God exalted him because he endured the sufferings.
They fell into this error because they neither read the apostle’s words correctly nor understood the force of those words.
“He humbled himself,” he says, “to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and granted him a name that is above every name,
so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bow.” “Do you see,” they say, “that he was exalted after the cross? Do you see that he received exaltation as a reward for his sufferings?”
For if he was exalted after the cross, why would John the Baptist proclaim, “He who came from above is above all”? He did not say that he would be above all, but that [?], and not that he would be.
Moreover, the Life-giver himself, while speaking with the Jews, said, “Truly, truly, I tell you, before Abraham came into being, I am.”
For he is eternal, and he was, and he will be. This is not confessed by you, but we render the worthy confession that is due.

From now on let Christ’s glory and the Spirit’s exaltation be proclaimed; let the Father’s power also be proclaimed. Let the Only-begotten also be exalted; let the Holy Spirit be glorified and praised.

And let no one suppose that we are disrupting the order when we speak first of the Son, then of the Spirit, and then of the Father; or when we speak first of the Son and the Father, and then of the Spirit.
For there is no order of rank in the immortal nature. I say there are no ranks, not because there is any disorder, but because there are no such ranks as rise above one another.
For example, when I said that God is without form, this does not signify any ugliness, but that he has no bodily form.
And when he is said to be without shape, it is not as though he lacks beauty of shape; rather, he is called without shape because he is bodiless.
Likewise, when I say that the divine nature is without an order of rank, I do not mean to indicate any disorder, but that there are no ranks there that rival one another.
I mentioned the Father first, not as first in rank, but as represented in thought, for he is the begetter of the Only-begotten and the root of the holy fruit.
And because he is eternal light, the offspring of eternal light is eternal light.

If someone dared now, here in this assembly of the orthodox, where there is the complete and correct confession of all knowledge, to name the Son before the Father in honor, would he not indeed be censured here by these orthodox believers?
And now, would he not dare to say to the church, “May Christ and his Father bless you”? Would he not indeed give an impression of disorder, since he did not honor the root first and then the fruit?
If someone said, “May the Son and the Father save you,” would he not indeed seem to be causing some confusion, and would you not be angry that he was disrupting the order?
But such opinions do not belong to the righteous, when someone looks to the truth and gives a just judgment,
and brings forward the apostolic ruling as victorious: to mention, without distinction, first the Son, then the Father, and then the Holy Spirit.
And listen to Paul, the great preacher. He writes to the Thessalonians: “May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, sanctify you.”
Not that the Son should sanctify first, and then the Father. Rather, Paul’s clear and enlightened spirit wished to show that there is no such ordering in holiness.
Rather, whoever is named first, the second shares his honor, and the third is neither diminished nor dishonored in any way.
For this reason he also brings the names forward, for he knows their undivided nature and their inseparable kingdom.
Let us ask Saint Paul: “Where did you get the grounds for speaking about God in this way, placing the Son before the Father—not in rank or power, but in words?”
And now let us say: “Why did you mention the Son first, and then the Father?” Let Paul answer, acting as his own defender and as the teacher of the church:
“I say nothing on my own authority. Christ establishes such teachings through me.” For he himself also says: “If you wish to seek proof of Christ, who speaks to you through me.”
“If Christ speaks through me, do not speak against the Lord’s words, and do not find fault with his teachings.”
But can you not understand and believe that Christ speaks through me? Listen to him himself when he speaks in his own person.
For if the names of the Holy Trinity stood under some [?] of subordination, and one were first in rank and power, and another second,
and another third, then the giver of life would not have called himself the truth either. “I am,” he says, “the truth”; yet he would have confused the order of truth.
And listen again to the giver of life: first [?] of himself, and then of the Father. “If you keep my commandments” (Greek: “if anyone keeps”), he says, “I and my Father will come” (and so on).
And since the heretics consider the Father’s rank to be higher, and regard the Son as a military commander serving the Father as king, let them now be asked:
Would a military commander dare to say, when speaking of royal matters, “I and the king will issue commands”?
For we must understand what is above us from what is familiar to us. Would a created nature dare to place itself before the uncreated nature,
and count itself alongside the incomparable one, whose equal it was not, taking precedence in the enumeration, and say, “I and the Father will come,
and make our dwelling with him”? For saying “I and the Father” made clear the distinction between the names, while “we will come and make our dwelling” proclaimed the equal honor of their deeds.
Likewise, in another place, when the apostle Philip said,
“Lord, show us your Father, and that is enough for us,” the giver of life answered: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip?” He gives an answer contrary to the question.
“Was it about you that I asked? Is it about you that I wish to learn? I say, ‘Show me your Father,’ not yourself.”
And what does he say in response? “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?”

If the Son is unlike him, how can the unlike one be known through one unlike him? Or how will you see the greater in the lesser, or the greater honor through the inferior, or the Creator through a servant?

“I have been with you so long,” he says. He did not say, “My Father is with you,” but “I am.” Through my being with you, the Father is with you. “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?”
He rightly said, “You have not known me.” The other says, “Show us,” but the Savior says, “Have you not known me?” He wanted to show that God is not seen but known.

And he adds to this: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? How, then, can you say, ‘Show us your Father’?” This is instead of saying, “How do you expect to see someone else [?]?”

For if I am in the Father and the Father is in me, and the Son is known through the Father and the Father through the Son, how can you say, “Show us your Father”? You want to leave me aside and see him as someone else.

“I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”—not as though the nature were somehow mixed together, or as though one cup stood inside another. He is not revealing any bodily connections, but an understanding of thought and word.

“I,” he says, “am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” The Father is not known without the Son, nor is the Son revealed without the Father, just as thought is known through the word, and the word is revealed through thought.
How could I know your thoughts except through the words you speak? Your words reveal your thoughts, and your thoughts give birth to your words.
And a person cannot understand words without thoughts, nor thoughts without the words that are born from those thoughts.
Likewise, the Father is known through the Son, and the Son is revealed through the Father. For this very reason the evangelist also says, “In the beginning was the Word.”
This is to show the birth without suffering and to explain the unity of being. What the word is in relation to thought, the only-begotten Word, who is God, is in relation to the Father.
These very things are marvelous. I will repeat once more what has been said. Our earlier words concerned this very matter, so that from what belongs to us you might learn what is above us.
While the word is still in the mind, it is invisible within the invisible, intelligible within the intelligible, incorporeal with the incorporeal.

And when the word wishes to come out, it first moves forward into the mouth, and from there it clothes itself with a voice. It does not take its voice from some other nature; rather, speech is articulated from the word itself.

And what is invisible by the nature of its parent puts on a voice and comes out, becoming known to everyone, though previously it was unknown. As it moves forward, it fills everyone, yet does not depart from the one who gave it birth.
Who among human beings, when speaking a word and teaching others, empties himself of that word?
And who would think, “Perhaps, while I put it into another person’s ears, I will leave my own mind naked and stripped bare”?
Did not the word go outside and yet remain there within? Did it not [?] many ears, yet not depart from the one who gave it birth?
Now, if a human word, when it moves and comes out of the mind, is not separated from the one who gave it birth,
would God the Word, who appeared in the world for our sake, leave his Father’s [?] bosom empty? Away with that, you sluggard! God forbid!
For myriads upon myriads hear the word, and it enters countless ears without being divided. Rather, it is whole with each person, all of it with everyone, and entirely in the mind.

And if the human word is entirely in the mind, whole with each person, and all of it with everyone, how can they say of the Father, “If he begot, then an outflow and a cutting occurred, and the indivisible was divided”?
Let the Giver of life say to them, “Search the Scriptures.” Search them, and do not read aimlessly, but investigate the depths of their meaning, putting them to searching examination.
For God set the Scriptures before us and withheld the meaning of their declarations. He gave the Scriptures, but did not lay bare their hidden interpretations.
Rather, he left them as a training ground for your races, to train the exercise of your mind, and to see whether you would serve the Scriptures or treat the Scriptures violently.
Just as God first set forth nature and concealed the skill: all materials and substances were set openly before us, while skill arose in human minds. So it is also with the Scriptures.
And to make my words still clearer: God set forth the natural substance of stones, but not a finished building.
He gave wheat; he did not make bread and set it before us. He gave grapes; he did not himself turn the grapes into wine.
He gave wool; he did not himself make clothing. He gave gold mixed with earth, but did not himself separate it from the earth.
Why? Because man was made in the image of God, God shares the work of creation: he himself makes things, and gives man the ability to fashion the work through skill.
For example, he gave man, who was made in the image of God, a share in assigning names to created beings.

He himself, as Creator, brought them from nonexistence into existence, and commanded his image to give them names. Likewise, he himself provided the materials and entrusted the fashioning of the work to skill.
Who first fashioned a plow to break up the earth with wood and iron and open a furrow, and made a yoke and a drawbar, and harnessed oxen for work with yoke-pins?
Wood and iron existed, but skill was nowhere among them. Who showed you, O man, to say, “I fashioned a plow in this way,” or that the hard substance of iron would soften in fire?
Who showed you how to sit and hammer it down from such thickness and make a tiny needle?
Who put it into your mind to make [?] for doors and locks, or to prepare beams and roofs for houses?
“You are asking a very foolish question,” he says. “I have God within me as the teacher of skills, and you ask, ‘Where did you learn?’”
And so, brothers, everywhere this human nature of ours, imitating its Lord, adorns natural things through skills.
If it remains within its limits, the image is good; but if it exceeds its limits, it is dishonored by its excess.
Here is an example: man learned to drive the ox, train the horse, tame the camel, and likewise the other animals that were given to serve us.
But through greed he also devised other mixtures contrary to nature, mating an ass with a horse, which was not according to God's will.
For in the beginning God said, “Let the earth bring forth four-footed animals and creeping things according to their kinds.” Greed devised the mixing of other combinations contrary to nature.
Therefore God, to punish this excess, made human greed barren.
For this reason the mule does not reproduce, because it is not among those that, when they came into being, heard, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.”
Nevertheless, he allows his image to do whatever it wishes, so that he may display its power, punish its excess, and expose its pride.

Again, unrestrained desire conceived the making of an image in human form. “Let me imitate God,” it says, “who made the human image, and make an image of the body.” And it forces nature through skill.
And because it heard that God took soil from the earth and made man, skill fell into perplexity, because it could not truly imitate its Lord. It then took refuge in devices and contrivances.
It gathers roots and flowers to prepare colors; it makes eyes resemble eyes, but they do not see. It measures out ears, but they do not hear.
It polishes the nostrils, but they do not smell. It [?] the mouth, but there is no voice on the lips. It fashions the form of the feet and thighs, but the feet neither move nor walk.
For by this he makes it clear that he allowed his image to do whatever it wished, but not to exceed its limits.
so that he may not become proud and fail to recognize his nature, or the freedom and salvation of his soul.
But nevertheless, so that he may learn that man was created from the earth, I wish to illustrate the Lord and Creator through another craft: the craft of physicians.
When a physician sees decay in the body, he puts an iron instrument to use and cuts away the decayed part.
And when he wishes to [?] the wound, bring about healing, and restore the wasted flesh to its proper size, he is not a creator who creates it anew.
Now, what craft can the image practice to imitate his Lord? He goes to the earth, from which the body was created, and makes medicines and poultices from it.
With one he removes the decay, and with another he rebuilds, and thus makes up what is lacking in the body.
And see the wonder: how God sits and watches them as though they were his children. And what does his watching make clear?
He does not watch in order to learn, but to train them. In this way the source of all good things instructs his own image.

As at the beginning, God placed before Adam all the wild animals, livestock, and birds, to see what he would call them—not so that the all-knowing one might learn, but so that he might train his image.
The desire to put [?] into the mind reveals the useful methods of building, carpentry, shipbuilding, metalworking, and weaving.
Looking at the stars, too, is not an idle activity. Observing the arrangement of the stars is useful to sailors,
as is attending to the rising of the stars and recognizing a time suitable for sailing—not to devise horoscopes, nor to introduce [?] tales of allotted destiny and fate,
but to follow the Lord’s words: “Let there be lights in the heavens, and let them shine upon the earth, and let them serve as signs, and for days and seasons.”
So that you may not suppose that the image discovers the means of doing everything on his own, the blessed Solomon makes this clear with a single statement.
“He gave me,” he says, “knowledge of whatever exists: an unerring understanding of the structure of the world and the arrangement of created things, the beginning, end, and middle of times,
the cycles of the elements and the arrangements of the stars, the habits of animals and the fury of wild beasts, plants of every kind and the powers of roots.
Whatever is hidden and whatever is manifest, whatever is visible and whatever is invisible, I, a man, came to know,” he says, instead of saying, “I, the image.”
And how? He says, “Wisdom, the master builder of everything, taught me.” But she taught you what is measurable, not what is immeasurable.
See how far the craft spread and advanced, beyond measure. It looked at human nature, and the image of God considered how the instrument of the mouth’s speech was formed.
He examined nature and imitated nature through his craft, devising a mechanism with many pipes joined together and interconnected.
And see what the craft does to imitate the work of the master builder: it constructs bellows that do not contain breath of their own,
but, by giving and receiving, opening and closing, draw in outside air in turn; then, from the two bellows, they send the breath into wind-carrying [?], and from there into all the pipes.
And he realizes that, although the air moves, it produces no melody. He devises a means for this too: arranging it with his fingers, he makes the melodies sound.
And where did this come from for you, O man? How did you learn to construct bellows that take in air, and to shape the filtered air into melodies with your fingers?
“You ask very foolishly,” he says. “Did I not already say that I am his image? Here I looked at my own nature and imitated it.”
For they see an outside breath entering me, and by repeatedly opening and closing these coverings, they take in the common mixture of air.
I see that two tubes give and receive air, as though through some [?] into my mouth. I see that air enters, but no speech comes forth unless the tongue passes between them and arranges the sounds.

I looked within myself and drew a comparison from my own nature, and through my own person I came to understand the Lord’s craftsmanship. As David also says, “Your knowledge has become wonderful in me.”
Here I looked within myself and glorified the craftsman. I became like my Lord, and through craftsmanship I visibly portrayed my nature.
The harp is not something evil; rather, it became an instrument for filthy songs. If it sang divine praises as it did at first, it would not be impure.
Although they are causes of unrestrained desire at feasts, nevertheless, if they were dedicated to God as at first, they would not be evil and impure.
As David also says, “Praise the Lord with the psaltery, with the lyre, with strings, with the harp, and with cymbals, with sweet sounds, with praise, with the tambourine, and with dancing.”
Now, if such a thing were not used for debauched revelry, nor again for the worship of idols, but one bore fruit for God by the same means through which one understood the art,
knowledge of the art would not deserve blame, if one acknowledged the Lord. The lyre would not deserve blame, if someone offered songs to God with the lyre.
For this reason, blessed David did not sing filthy songs with the lyre, but offered sacred praises to God and put demons to flight.
When the evil spirit tormented Saul, the Scriptures say that David played the lyre, and Saul found relief.
Do you see that every art has been fashioned for God’s pleasure? There would be no evil if everything were done according to God’s will.
What, then, did I wish to show, that I passed from speaking about God to such matters—to craftsmanship and to resembling the image of one’s Creator?
It was to show that I am examining the Lord’s utterance and exposing the heretics’ groundless opinions. The Lord’s utterance? Which one?
“Hypocrites,” he says, “you know how to interpret the appearance of the sky. You know the arts, you have understood wisdom, and yet you insult the craftsman of all things?”

You became like your Lord through your craftsmanship and made whatever you wished, for you were established in the image and likeness of the Creator. Yet do you proclaim that the Creator is unlike the one who begot him?
I freed you who were subject to sins, and do you call me, who am Lord of all, into subjection?
“Yes,” they say, “for it is written that the Son will be subjected.” We have already spoken about this according to our ability—or rather, by the power of God.
For these words are not ours, but God’s. Remember them. Nevertheless, even now let us direct a few rebukes against them.
Let us examine the statement. In the world to come and in the resurrection, where you say that the Son will be subjected, will you not indeed become a sun and an angel?
“At the resurrection of the dead,” he says, “men do not take wives, nor do women become wives of men, but they will be like angels.”
Will you then rise above your present rank, while the Son descends from his lordship to a lower position?
Have you not heard from Paul? “Creation,” he says, “was subjected to futility, and creation itself groans and suffers labor pains until now.”
If created things—that is, heaven and earth and everything else—were subjected to humanity’s futility,
for he calls humanity futile because it corrupted the image and descended into the likeness of beasts, as he also says elsewhere, “Vanity of vanities; everything is vanity.”
And David says, “Every living person is altogether vanity.” Now created things were subjected to man, who corrupted the image. And how were they subjected?
For the sun rises for the unworthy, the rains fall, springs flow for those without grace, and the earth bears fruit for the ungrateful.
And thus created things were subjected to vanity, and not willingly. For if it depended on their will, they would not submit to the unworthy, but because of the one who did not subject them in hope.

For created things themselves, he says, will also be freed from slavery to corruption into the glorious freedom of the Son of God. But if created things will then be freed, will the Son enter into slavery?
Examine the Scriptures, and do not slander. Examine them, and do not search aimlessly. Examine them, believe, and do not dispute.
Where did you learn to say, “Did the Son exist before he was begotten, or did he not?” Where did you learn that begetting and making are the same?
Did Peter teach you this, or did Paul expound it, or did the Life-giver hand it down? Read the Scriptures.

You do not even stand by what you say. For when you ask, “Did he exist before he was begotten, or did he not?” you are already speaking falsely, because what you ask about is not what you acknowledge.
First acknowledge that the Son was begotten, and then ask about existence and nonexistence. But you deny the facts and make the words [?].
Why demand an explanation of something whose begetting you do not grant? “Did the Son exist,” he says, “before he was begotten, or did he not?”
First grant me that he was begotten. First seal a written pledge that he was begotten, and then ask how. But you deny the nature itself and subject the words to investigation and inquiry.
You say that making and begetting are the same. Yet even for me they are not the same unless the distinction between the two first becomes clear, and then their meanings agree.
For if I say that looking and seeing are the same, one thing will be expressed. But if I say that hearing and seeing are the same, then I seem to have assigned to hearing what belongs to the eyes.
And where did you learn that making and begetting are the same for God? For if you acknowledged that he was begotten and made, then you could rightly say that they are the same.
But if you never acknowledge that he was begotten, how can you consider begetting and making the same?
And you will be found not only to introduce empty words, but also to be entirely devoid of truth.
And now we must learn why the heretic cleverly argues that making and begetting are the same. For God, he says, is a simple and diffuse essence,
and is not like us. For we beget with one set of organs and work with another: we beget with the reproductive organs and work with our hands.
God is not like that, but is simple and diffuse, and without form. In the same way that he begets, he also makes.
And now, since you promise to demonstrate the properties of invisible things, puffed up with improper cleverness, I will show you from visible things whether works are done in the same way.
Bring the visible hand into consideration, so that through these visible things a demonstration of invisible things may also be brought forward.
For whatever is done by one and the same hand is not called one and the same work, nor does it display one and the same activity.
For example: with this one and the same hand I built and demolished. Are the two the same?
For they also say that we beget in one way and work in another. I too say, following the same example, that we build and demolish with the same hand.
And we strike and smooth with the same hand. We push and throw down and raise up those who have fallen with the same hand. And we count and undo the count with the same hand.
And now, are building and tearing down the same? Or striking and smoothing, and the other things, one by one?
Are these not the words of fools and unsuitable fables? Would Paul's thoughts not groan at this? And would Peter not be angry at mixing such words into the teaching?
Have you denied Christ and begun learning from others? Have you not heard [?] him who said, “Whoever is ashamed of me and my words, I too will deny him”?
For many, many times I confess Christ but am ashamed of his words, just as you yourself will feel regret
when you come to discourses about God and hear the name of the Father and of the Son, and are ashamed of the words,
and say such things as these: “Did the one who cannot suffer really beget? Did he beget at all? And if that is so, it must have been by an outflow and a division.”
Do you see that you are ashamed of the words? He addresses his saying to such people: “Whoever is ashamed of my words, I too will deny him.”
Oh, the folly! They became hunters of words alone, and not true investigators of realities. Vanity, guilty before the Lord, has ruined and corrupted everything.
What I have said many times, I will say now as well: the chiefs and leaders of these heresies are known, and the holy church has never accepted heretical teaching.
If you can ever recall that someone of this name became a leader of the church's religion, you must bring him forward.
But I know that you cannot identify who introduced this sect, which you call a sect, though it is not a sect but the truth,

which the apostles themselves preached from the beginning. After them, the Council of Nicaea confirmed the same thing, so that it might be clear that this was the faith of the whole world, the universal faith.
But among that great multitude of bishops gathered in one place, only seven bishops did not agree, and the exiles and outcasts were cast aside.
And the whole world agreed, because they were of the mixture seasoned by the apostles.
And see these wonders: the whole new world resembled the Old Testament, just as there Abraham, who had greater faith, armed himself
with his three hundred and eighteen servants born in his household, and routed five kings of the Assyrians who had come against the land of the Palestinians.
Following the same pattern and number, Christ too gathered to himself three hundred and eighteen bishops to wage war against the heretics.

Three hundred and eighteen servants born in his household were with Abraham, and he went against the foreigners. Although there were also many other servants bought with silver, he showed the close bond of the servants born in his household.

Likewise, Christ did not gather everyone together indiscriminately, but those born in the household of the faith. And they proclaimed the true one from the true one, the living one from the living one, the light from the light.
What separation do you suppose there is between light and light? What difference between life and life? What difference in form between truth and truth?
And what is still more wonderful is that the Father is called light. John says, “God is light,” while the Son is described with the added qualification, “He was the true light.”
The Father is simply called light without qualification, because of the belief about him, and because the audacious heretics muster against the divinity of the Son.
Although, if anyone [?] dares, he directs insults at the Father, nevertheless the Scriptures reveal what is manifest in clear words, and establish what is doubtful by the truth.
The Father is called light, without an added qualification, because the proclamation alone is sufficient to make him known. The Son too is named light.

So that you may not think that he is intelligible and genuine light, while this one is some visible and [?] light, he strengthens the statement with this addition: “He was,” he says, “the true light.”
And again, so that no one may say, “Just as the sun is light and the moon is light, but one is a great light and the other a small one,
so also the Father is some great light and the Son a small one,” Isaiah goes before him as a herald and sets things right:
“Land of Zebulun,” he says, “and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the river Jordan: the people who sat in darkness saw a great light.”
If the Father is called a great light, behold, the Son too is named a great light. Great is the one who begets, and great is the one begotten; great is the root, and great is the fruit.
Great is the light, and great is the radiance of the light. I recognize no great and small there, but only the great. I know the Trinity as united.
The Father is great, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “You are God, great and everlasting.”
Paul also says of the Son: “We await the blessed hope and the appearing of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ.” And David says:
“Great is the Lord, and great is his power.” Surely he is not one thing and his power another? And the apostle testifies that the Son is his power: “Christ,” he says, “is the power of God.”
Again the prophet says, “Great is our Lord,” as though to say that the Father is great, and his power—the Holy Spirit—is great.
As the giver of life said to the apostles: “Stay and remain in Jerusalem until you receive power from on high.”

But see how cleverly the opponents argue. “This,” they say, “is a power that distributes the greatness of the promises, and nowhere is it written that the Spirit is God, but rather the pledge of the inheritance.”
And pay attention: a pledge is a part of the gift, not the entire gift, but a part of the whole.
“It is written,” they say, “in the Apostle: ‘You were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance.’ Do you see,” they say, “that he is a gift and not God?”
Now, if you find that the Father too is called a portion and an inheritance, will you follow the words there too, rather than their meaning?
For both the inheritance and the portion are gifts from the giver, and not the one who gives the inheritance himself.
And if calling the Holy Spirit a pledge causes you to stumble, then when you hear that the Father too is a portion of the inheritance, will you direct your blasphemy against him as well?
Pay close attention: he did not say “an inheritance,” but “a portion of the inheritance.” And David bears witness:
“The Lord,” he says, “is the portion of my inheritance.” Thus, just as he is a portion of the inheritance, so also the Spirit is the pledge of the inheritance.
If saying “a portion of the inheritance” makes the Father small, then calling the Spirit “the pledge of the inheritance” does the same.
And elsewhere David says, “The Lord is my portion in the land of the living.” A portion is a part of something, and not the entire whole.
Now, if you are a hunter of words and not an examiner of their meaning, nothing will then prevent you from blaspheming God, whom you think you are glorifying.
“The Lord,” he says, “is the portion of my inheritance,” and “The Lord is my portion in the land of the living.” Is it necessary to explain why the whole power is called a portion and an inheritance?
For we worship God of our own free will, and one person has taken pleasure in foolishness, and another has fallen; he becomes the portion of the believers who choose him.
Something like this: “Let the Levites,” he says, “have no portion of land, for the Lord is their portion, whom they chose.”
And the prophet makes it clear that he chose God of his own will, and not under compulsion. “The Lord,” he says, “is my portion.”
If God loses nothing of his divinity when he is called a portion, likewise the Holy Spirit loses nothing of his divinity when he is called a pledge.
Let us henceforth cast aside the [?] confusion and accept the apostolic faith.
How long will you set up scales and weigh the divine words? You have thoughts like weights in your mind; weigh the Savior’s gifts.

Consider which belong to the flesh and which to the divinity, which to his dignity and which to the dispensation, so that it may not also be said of you, “The scales of Canaan are in his hand, scales of injustice.”
And the other saying would apply to you: “The sons of men are vain; they sin in the scales.” You hold the beam of the scales and distort the just balance.
Be attentive to the equal weights of the Giver of life; pay attention and look closely. “I and my Father,” he says, “are one.” Where, then, is any inequality?
Look at the equal weights of the divine word. “Whoever has seen me,” he says, “has seen my Father.” Where, then, is anything that would tilt downward or pull upward?
See the Father who sets free, the Son who sets free, and the Spirit who sets free. “Unless the Son sets you free,” he says, “you are slaves.”
And Paul says, “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set us free.” If the Father sets free, and the Son sets free, and the Spirit sets free.
But may all of us be freed from the yoke of sins, escape the yoke of the heretics, uphold the steadfast faith, and give glory to the Holy Trinity forever.
